title: An Unknown Corner of the World
mood: A girl stows away to a far fort, where Enders walk out of the grass, and teaches herself to wait.

hero.alt: A design sheet of the Enders against a height scale: tall gray giants with long claws tower over a small human figure, and one chest is drawn split open around a burning orange core.

segs.t: Lesley was still standing in the street when the rain thinned and the soldiers came up the hill. They were the Shield of Dawnbreak, the army that fought the Enders.
One of them knelt in front of her. He wound a field dressing around her head, over the left eye.
“Anyone else in there?”
She shook her head.
He tied a paper tag to her wrist. “Wait at the bottom of the hill with the others. Somebody will come for you.”
Over the bay, the black cloud was gone.
“Where do they come from?”
“Who?”
“The Enders.”
He pointed down the road out of the city. “Out there. That’s where they come in groups.”
Down the hill, soldiers were loading trucks.
“Last truck for the far stations!” one shouted.
The far stations were Shield forts guarding the last towns beyond the city.
Lesley pulled the tag off her wrist and dropped it in the mud.
She climbed over the tailboard of the last truck and folded herself small between two crates. The engine started.
Far from Terrinia. The years after.
Three days later the road ended at a Shield station.
The station was a ring of earth walls and gun pits on a plain of gray grass. It was an unknown corner of the world.
When the crates came off, she slid behind the stack in the storeroom. The trucks left at dawn.
The sergeant found her that afternoon. He was a heavy man with a burned hand.
“Who are you with?”
“Nobody.”
“Then you go back on the next convoy.”
“When is it?”
“Months.” He rubbed his face. “I’ve got a boy your size in the city. He still can’t tie his boots. This is no place for him, and it’s no place for you.”
The medic swapped the dressing for a black patch.
The station had no clocks. That night she lay on her bunk and listened for the ticking. It did not come. She was still listening at dawn.
The convoy came at the turn of the season. Every soldier had a letter for the drivers but her. When the trucks pulled out, she was lying flat under the armory floorboards.
The sergeant lifted a board and looked down at her a long time.
“If you’re staying,” he said, “you work.”
He gave her the rifles to clean. Her hands were quick with small parts. Nobody asked where she had learned that.

At dawn she took the oldest rifle up on the wall, empty. Rounds were for Enders. She stood on an ammunition box to see over and aimed at the grass. She held the aim until her arms shook, then held it longer.
Once a week at noon, the gunners test-fired the wall guns. The sergeant let her fire one round with them, at a fence post in the grass.
“One,” he said. “Let’s see how you like the kick.”
The kick knocked her off the box. Her shoulder went black, then yellow. The next week she got back on.
She was the only child at the station. In a raid she was meant to go to the bunker. She went up the wall instead. The first time, the sergeant carried her down. After that he only looked.
The first raid she saw came at dusk. Three Enders walked out of the grass, taller than the wall. Rounds sparked off their shells. They kept walking.
One raised an arm over the east gun pit. As the arm came down, its chest came apart in plates. A core burned inside, and the gunner’s face went bright with it.
He fired into the opening. The Ender folded and fell, and the other two drew back into the grass.
The chest had stayed open for less time than it took to say her name.
It opens when it hits,
she thought.
Only then.
That night the gunner chalked a stroke on the armory door, beside the others. The station kept its count there.
Nobody at the station taught her anything. On the wall at dawn she aimed at the grass and counted under her breath.
Wait. Wait. Now.
The youngest soldier stood the dawn watch beside her. He counted out loud, too: the days to his leave.
“Forty-one,” he said one morning, by way of hello. “You never talk, you know that? Why don’t you ever talk?”
Lesley did not lower the rifle.
“Bullets are the only language the enemy understands.”
He laughed. Then he saw her face, and stopped.
That night he asked her to play cards. She went back to the rifles.
If I don’t know him,
she thought,
it won’t matter when he’s gone.
By then the sergeant gave her five rounds a week. The fence post was more hole than post.
One dawn she was on the wall with that week’s five rounds in her pocket. She no longer needed the box. Then an Ender came out of the grass. It crossed the wall in one stride. The earth shook.
“Fall back!” shouted the sergeant.
The soldiers fell back to the bunker line, firing. Lesley lay flat on the wall walk and loaded.
The youngest soldier slipped at the foot of the ladder and went down in the mud. The Ender turned to him.
Wait.
It raised its arm. Lesley laid her sight on its chest, on the seam she had watched for years.
Wait.
The arm came down. The chest plates split, and the core glowed.
Now.
She fired once. The round went into the core, and the glow went out. Its arm struck the mud beside the soldier, and the rest of it came down across half the yard.
Then there was only the wind in the grass.
The sergeant came out first. He looked at the dead Ender, at the soldier sitting up in the mud, then up at the wall.
“Report,” he said.
“Another threat eliminated.”
She said it flat, the way the soldiers spoke into the radio. The whole station stared at her.
That night the sergeant held out the chalk. Lesley made her own stroke on the armory door.
Outside, the youngest soldier held out the cards. “Twelve days,” he said. “Then I’m gone. One game.”
Lesley went past him to her bunk. She lay down and slept. When she woke, the sun was high.
More,
she thought.
More strokes.
The Shield took her as a soldier. The smallest uniform it had still covered her hands.
“Date of birth?” asked the clerk.
She gave it. She did not think of it again.
Her record went up the line ahead of her. New badges came by convoy. She sewed them on herself.

The last towns emptied as people drew back to Terrinia, humanity’s final bastion. One by one the far stations closed. Hers was among the last. The armory door stayed behind. A long row of the strokes on it was hers.
Terrinia. Later.
She came back in the upper ranks of the Shield, the youngest anyone there had heard of.
She walked down the street of repair shops once. It still ran downhill to the bay. Most of it was new. In one window a clock was ticking.
She did not stop.
An officer had her file open on his desk.
“Terrinia’s research base,” he said. “Two chief scientists, and a child they’ve taken in. You’re the best young shot we have. Keep them alive.”
“Understood.”
She took it like any other mission. She was there to protect important people. Nothing more.
Two people in white coats waited at the base gate. Lesley saluted them.
The woman smiled and held out her hand anyway. Lesley looked at it.
From behind the woman’s white coat, a small face was looking up at her.
